title_original: Echoes of Magritte Are Everywhere in London’s Galleries Right Now
excerpt_original: Surrealism abounds, from Nicole Eisenman at Sadie Coles to Louis Fratino at David Zwirner.

blocks.text: When Frieze Week arrives in London, there is always one exhibition that you’d be embarrassed to admit you missed. This year, that honor goes to Gagosian for its immaculately produced ode to René Magritte and his sprawling influence. The smash-hit show has received some 10,000 visitors since opening September 24, with lines often stretching around the block.

blocks.alt: a painting that in its top half appears to be daytime with blue skies and clouds but below seems to be a house shown at night with its lighits on and the mysterious silhouette of a man in a hat looking at the horizon, we can see him from behind

blocks.text: René Magritte, The Empire of Light (1961). Photo: Prudence Cuming Associates Ltd, Heidi Horten Collection, © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, London.

Featuring a whopping 120 works by the Surrealist master and 45 of contemporary art’s biggest names—including Jeff Koons , Glenn Ligon , Jordan Wolfson , and Issy Wood —” This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte ,” through December 12, was always going to be big deal. Less predictable is how the show captures a prevailing mood. It stuck in my head, its themes and motifs reverberating throughout a recent gallery hop in Mayfair and East London. Again and again, I was reminded of what seems to be the Gagosian show’s central thesis: that a once-novel strain of Surrealism is now the dominant artistic lens on our world.

Here are just a few of the surprising parallels I encountered.
Impossibility

blocks.alt: a man in a waiter's uniform stands in front of stone henge and looks up at a sky full of stars, planets and galaxies

blocks.text: Nicole Eisenman, The Waiter (2026). Image: Katie Morrison, © Nicole Eisenman, courtesy the artist and Sadie Coles HQ, London.

Just a few streets from Gagosian, an exhibition of 10 new works by Nicole Eisenman at Sadie Coles (through November 21) offered the same incongruity that characterizes many Magritte masterpieces. The Waiter (2026) is an epic, 11-by-21-foot spectacle in which high-definition planets and swirling galaxies float above the lichen-covered slabs of Stonehenge . The kicker is the lone figure of a waiter, his shirt collar open and bowtie limp as though at the end of his shift. What is he doing there? The man gazes up, as confused by the cosmos as we are by his impossibly mundane presence within it.

blocks.alt: two paintings side by side, on the left is a multicolored, monstrous figure that appears to melt and on the right is a painting in whichh a large melty while fantastical figure stands over a boxy car containing lots of ICE agents, they are patrolling a vast empty parking lot

blocks.text: From left to right: René Magritte, Pictorial Content (1947). Photo: Margaret Carrigan. Nicole Eisenman, Parking Lot of Violent Forces and Depressive Positions (2026). Image: Katie Morrison, © Nicole Eisenman, courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, London..

The empty, flat expanse of Magritte paintings like The Flowers of the Journey (1926) and The Leader of the Band (1955) takes on new meaning in Eisenman’s Parking Lot of Violent Forces and Depressive Positions (2026). The effect is ominous, yes, but also absurd, infusing irony into the Philip Guston -style satire, in which ICE agents pile into a clown car to patrol the desolate, gray surrounds of a strip mall. A monstrous, dripping figure, apparently composed of exhaust fumes, brings to mind the same oozing forms found in Magritte’s Pictorial Content (1947), one of the cruder images he made during his short-lived vache period.
Ambiguity

blocks.alt: two paintings side by side, on the left is a surreal painting of a man in a bowler hat seeming to inhabit a green outdoor space and a brick-walled space simultaneously, on the right an image of men crowded onto a subway platform

blocks.text: From left to right: René Magritte, The Commonplace (1964) Image: © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, London. Louis Fratino, Summer in the city (2026). Image: Kerry McFate, © Louis Fratino, courtesy David Zwirner.

Distorted spatial logic gives a claustrophobic feel to the canvases of Louis Fratino , who has prepared 12 new paintings for “ Prose ” at David Zwirner , through October 31. Summer in the City (2026) uses an unusual vantage point to divide the picture plane, layering the disparate lives of urban strangers and leaving its central figure as dislocated as the one in Magritte’s The Commonplace (1964).

blocks.alt: two paintings side by side, on the left is a green-tinged painting of two naked men in a bath and on the right is a more lime green-tinged painting of three faces closed in together and looking at something

blocks.text: From left to right: Louis Fratino, The green bath (2026). Photo: Kerry McFate, © Louis Fratino, courtesy David Zwirner. Victor Man, Titiriteros (2023). Image: def image, © Victor Man, courtesy Gagosian.

Fratino’s running interest in everyday domesticity turns a little sickly in The green bath (2026), where two languid nudes sit entwined. It is impossible not to think of the similarly emerald-tinged palette preferred by Salman Toor , who is having his solo European museum debut at the Courtauld , until January 10. His paintings seduce us into a dreamy otherworld, filled with queer intimacies that have too often been pushed into the shadows. A more sinister comparison is Titiriteros (2023) by the ever-mysterious Victor Man , included in the Gagosian survey. Glowing lime green and with all the moody atmosphere of an El Greco , it closes in on three women burning a piece of paper that bears the artist’s initials. As in Fratino’s painting, expressionless faces and averted eyes leave the viewer guessing as to the composition’s true meaning.
Reinvention

blocks.alt: three image side by side, on the left a painting of disembodied calves wearing shoes and fancy dress, in the middle a decorated pink high heel and on the right a sculpture made of two deconstructed high heels

blocks.text: From left to right: René Magritte, The Triumphant March (1948). Image: © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, London, courtesy Brachot Gallery. M: Alex Da Corte, Slow Graffiti (2017). Image: Joseph Hu, © Alex Da Corte, courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, London. R: Installation view of Adam Lewis Jacob’s “Short Vamps for Long Wear” at Neven, 2026. Image: Dominique Croshaw, courtesy of the artist and Neven, London.

Vast, central podiums filling the main rooms of the Gagosian show are not to be overlooked. Many of the smaller objects assembled call for close examination, as is the case with Alex da Corte ‘s Slow Graffiti (2017). Sexualized objects like the high-heeled shoe have long held a fetishistic appeal for the Surrealists, and Da Corte’s mini, winged stiletto installation flattens the distinction between real life and fantasy.

In Magritte’s The Triumphal March (1948), meanwhile, a disembodied calf in a high-heeled shoe gains a life of its own while donning pieces of fancy dress. At Neven gallery in Bethnal Green, Adam Lewis Jacob has broken apart used stilettos to build wacky new constructions that still contain telling signifiers of their former life for his show “ Short Vamps for Long Wear ,” until October 24.
Doubling

blocks.alt: two images side by side, on the left is a bench made of plump pink fabric with a marshmallow, puffy texture and on the right is a grey, stuffed fabric figure slumped on a chair

blocks.text: From left to right: Charlotte Kingsnorth, Marshmallow Bench (2026). Image: Jack Elliot Edwards, courtesy the artist and Rose Easton, London. R: Sarah Lucas, SLAG (2022). Image: Steve Russell Studios, © Sarah Lucas, courtesy Sadie Coles HQ, London.

A short walk away, at Rose Easton , the group show “ Lumps and Bumps ” was inspired by the Comme des Garçons Spring/Summer 1997 collection “Body Meets Dress, Dress Meets Body,” but has plenty of incidental callbacks to the Magritte survey. Through December 12, it features the newly commissioned Marshmallow Bench by Charlotte Kingsnorth , a plump, pink leather sofa with an uncomfortably corporeal quality.

For Magritte, too, the body can double as an object, as in works from the Gagosian show like The Music Lesson (1965), in which an ear is attached to a bell, and The Red Model (1935), in which shoes become feet. In his The Art of Living (1967), a head balloons, becoming ridiculously oversized. A similar lack of constraint governs the slumped, stuffed figure, its bulging seams all awry, in Sarah Lucas ‘s SLAG (2022), also included in the show.

The Gagosian survey’s oldest work dates to 1926, exactly one century ago, but many of the later pieces were made in the past five years. If Magritte’s influence has undoubtedly endured through the decades, my recent gallery hop left me with the sense that his eye for the enigmatic and absurd is more relevant now than ever.
